everyharness

Generate a coding-agent plugin for every harness from one config file.

v1.0.0 · stable config schema · not yet on npm

The problem

Every harness wants its own manifest.

You wrote a plugin and people liked it. Then they asked for it in their own coding agent.

Claude Code reads .claude-plugin/plugin.json. Codex reads .codex-plugin/plugin.json. Gemini CLI wants gemini-extension.json, OpenCode wants a JavaScript plugin file, Pi wants a TypeScript extension, and Hermes wants YAML plus a Python init file. Each format drifts on its own schedule, and every release means editing all of them by hand.

Superpowers, the plugin this tool was extracted from, carried nine hand-maintained manifest files and four distinct bootstrap mechanisms. A missed edit ships as a user's broken install.

Sources: docs/BROCHURE.md §What you get · docs/superpowers/specs/2026-08-10-everyharness-design.md

What you get

One file describes your plugin. Everything else is generated.

everyharness.yaml is the source of truth. everyharness generate writes the rest, and you commit it.

Native files for 12 harnesses

Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI, Cursor, Copilot CLI, OpenCode, Pi, Kimi Code, Hermes, Devin CLI, Factory Droid, and Grok Build CLI, through 11 adapters. Antigravity is on the roadmap.

Install docs, written for you

Every generation emits an install page for each adapter and a component support matrix, so your users get accurate steps for their agent.

Bootstrap wiring

The session-start hooks and pointer files that make your discovery skill load automatically, synthesized from your skill list or pointed at a skill you wrote.

A scaffold and a converter

init creates a working config in an empty directory. import converts an existing Claude-format plugin, carrying over its metadata and its skill, command, agent, hook, and MCP-server entries.

Drift detection for CI

validate loads your config with the same rules generation uses, then checks every generated file against the recorded hashes. Distinct exit codes for config, schema, and drift failures.

Proven on a real plugin

The dogfood test regenerates eight of superpowers' hand-maintained manifests from one config and compares them semantically. It runs against a local superpowers checkout.

Using it

Three commands, from a clean directory.

A real session in a directory named demo-plugin (the scaffold names the plugin after its directory):

$ node everyharness/dist/cli.js init
created: everyharness.yaml
created: skills/getting-started/SKILL.md
Generated 32 files for initialization
Next: edit everyharness.yaml, then re-run everyharness generate

$ node everyharness/dist/cli.js generate
warning: [kimi] kimi sessionStart requires a named bootstrap
skill; generate mode is not supported on kimi
Generated 32 files for 11 harness(es): claude-code, cursor, codex,
devin, kimi, gemini, opencode, pi, hermes, agent-plugins-1.0,
agents-marketplace

$ node everyharness/dist/cli.js validate
validate: clean

Those 32 files include the Claude, Codex, Gemini, OpenCode, Pi, and Hermes plugin files, eleven install docs, the support matrix, and the bootstrap hook wiring. You commit them; validate keeps them honest from then on.

Running it

The maintainer's guardrails.

You own a plugin repo and want releases to stay coherent.

  • CI. Run everyharness validate on every push. Exit code 1 is a config error, 2 is a schema violation, 3 is drift: a generated file hand-edited or deleted since the last generate. An edited everyharness.yaml whose outputs were never regenerated passes, so regenerate after every config change.
  • Install checks. everyharness test runs two offline tiers inside a shared container: it parses every generated manifest and checks referenced paths, then performs a real install into each harness CLI and asserts the CLI enumerates the plugin's skills. This catches a manifest that parses but is wired to the wrong place.
  • Releases. everyharness bump 1.2.3 rewrites the version everywhere it lives, regenerates all manifests, then audits for stray version strings. It replaces per-repo bump scripts.

Costs and limits, by who bears them

  • Author: unpublished on npm; every install is a clone-and-build until the package reaches the registry.
  • Maintainer: test needs Docker and pulls a ~15 GB linux/amd64 container image on first use.
  • Maintainer: Kimi Code, Cursor, and Devin CLI have no offline install check and are reported as skip. Author: Kimi also requires a named bootstrap skill.

Sources: docs/BROCHURE.md §Running it, §Limitations · checks/run-checks.sh · src/bump.ts · README

Who it's for

Fit, by role. And who should wait.

For plugin authors who ship one plugin to several coding agents, and for maintainers who want manifest drift caught by CI instead of by bug reports.

A plugin that targets one harness and will stay there is better served by its single hand-written manifest; this tool earns its keep at two harnesses and up. Teams that want npm install everyharness should wait: the package is not yet on the registry, so every install is a clone-and-build.

Sources: docs/BROCHURE.md §Who it's for · README top note

Get started

Two doors.

Plugin author: try it on your plugin

Clone and build the repo (Node 20 or newer), then run import in your existing Claude-format plugin and generate. The brochure doc has the exact commands.

Maintainer: wire the guardrails

Add validate to CI, run test before releases, adopt bump in place of your version script. The README's Configuration section documents every knob.

Contributing? The design record lives in docs/superpowers/specs/ and docs/superpowers/plans/.
